title: Concurrency: how would you diagnose a race condition that occurs once a day?
description: Learn a systematic approach to reproducing, capturing, and fixing intermittent race conditions in production C# applications.

data.text: A race condition that happens once a day is one of the hardest bugs to fix. The usual debugging techniques — breakpoints, single-stepping, and local reproduction — often fail because timing changes when you attach a debugger. A systematic investigation strategy is more valuable than any single tool.

Start by defining the observable failure: corrupted state, a duplicate record, a thrown exception, or an incorrect calculation. The failure tells you which shared resource is contested and narrows the search space.

Because the bug is rare, you need to amplify the conditions that expose it. Run multiple instances in parallel, inject artificial delays, or lower the contention threshold so the window of vulnerability widens.

data.title: Amplifying a race with delays
data.content: This simplified example shows two threads updating a shared counter without synchronization. Adding Thread.Sleep widens the race window for demonstration; in production you would use this pattern only in a controlled test.

data.title: Do not use Thread.Sleep in production
data.text: Sleep only in test harnesses. In production, capture production artifacts: ETW traces, EventSource events, and structured logs with correlation IDs.
When you cannot reproduce locally, collect evidence from production without stopping the service. The goal is to record the exact sequence of events that led to the corrupted state.

data.title: Production steps
items: Instrument the suspicious code path with structured logs that include request IDs, thread IDs, and timestamps.
Enable `System.Diagnostics` EventSource listeners and capture ETW traces with `dotnet-trace`.
Look for overlapping timestamps on the same resource: two writes within microseconds are a strong signal.
If the bug involves a database, enable SQL Server audit or PostgreSQL log_statement to see interleaved transactions.

data.text: Once you know which resource is contested, choose the light-weight synchronization primitive that fits the access pattern. Do not default to `lock` for every scenario; reader/writer locks, `SemaphoreSlim`, and lock-free algorithms have specific trade-offs.

data.title: Common fixes
items: Use `lock` (or `Monitor.Enter/Exit`) for simple mutual exclusion on reference types.
Use `Interlocked` for atomic updates to numeric or reference fields.
Prefer immutable data structures or message passing to avoid shared mutable state.

data.title: Thread-safe counter
data.content: This version uses Interlocked to guarantee that the decrement is atomic.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Race conditions require evidence: logs, traces, and dumps — not guesswork.
Amplify timing windows in test environments to make the bug reproducible.
Pick the lightest synchronization primitive that solves the problem.
Immutable data and message passing eliminate many races by design.
data.takeaway: Diagnose with production telemetry first, then reproduce in a controlled test, then apply the simplest correct fix.
